Which Agent’s Skill Should Change?
Group-Relative Credit Assignment for Evolving Multi-Agent Teams

Yanan Ma Yang Wang , David Le , Chenhan Yuan , Yizheng Sun , Guangwei Zhang , Chenghao Xiao , Chenghua Lin , Imon Banerjee   Mayo Clinic,  University of Manchester,  Alibaba Token Hub, Alibaba Group,  Shanghai University of Finance and Economics ††thanks: Corresponding authors’ email addresses: {ma.yanan;banerjee.imon}@mayo.com. Our code is available at https://github.com/yananma1029/GRSE-Skills.
Abstract

Cooperative language-model agents can improve without weight updates by revising reusable skills, but only if a shared team reward is traced to the responsible agent and skill. Existing methods credit the skills present in each trajectory, yet presence is not responsibility: a harmful skill active in successful runs still earns positive credit. We present GRSE, Group-Relative Skill Evolution, which assigns behavioral credit by comparison: inspired by GRPO, it executes each question several times under the same skill libraries and contrasts the executions to credit agent–skill pairs, with structured diagnosis of failures. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills, the closest prior method, on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions (+6.7+6.7 and +3.2+3.2 F1). Its gains rest on better-grounded retrieval rather than answers given without evidence, and its learned skills transfer between the multi-hop tasks. GRSE is robust to corrupted libraries: starting from planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and recovers the score of a clean library (+6.3+6.3 points), whereas MASkills misattributes two and falls below its starting point.

1 Introduction

Language-model agents increasingly work in teams: one agent collects evidence, another reasons over it, and the team is judged by a single outcome (Cemri et al., 2026; Ghareeb et al., 2026; Tran et al., 2025; Dang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026b; Hong et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023). Improving such a team requires answering a credit assignment question: which agent’s behavior, and which step of it, produced a success or a failure? The question is classical in multi-agent reinforcement learning, where a shared reward is decomposed with difference rewards or counterfactual baselines (Wolpert and Tumer, 2001; Foerster et al., 2018; Rashid et al., 2020), and it has recently been posed for language-model teams as automated failure attribution (Zhang et al., 2025). A wrong answer may stem from evidence collection, an incomplete handoff, or downstream reasoning (Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025), and the agent whose output is wrong is often not the agent whose behavior needs to change. For example, reasoner answers wrongly when the retriever misses the evidence.

We study this problem in a setting where model parameters stay fixed and each agent’s behavior is specified by natural-language skills, reusable procedures that the agent reads and follows (Zhao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023; Alzubi et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026). Skills make behavior editable, so credit becomes actionable: once responsibility is located, the responsible procedure can be revised. Existing experience- and skill-learning methods, however, assign credit coarsely, which often distill lessons from whole trajectories, and mainly focus on single-agent setting (Shinn et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2026; Ouyang et al., 2026). Meanwhile MASkill, the recent two-agent SOTA, credits each skill from single trajectory in isolation (Yao et al., 2026). However, without a contrast, a skill that is present in every execution also receives credit for the successes it did not cause: in our robustness study, MASkills raises the utility of a planted harmful skill over three iterations, whereas our method labels it harmful and prunes it (Appendix C). Comparison between executions already guide experience distillation, skill refinement, and prompt optimization (Cai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Zehle, 2026), but they have not been used to localize a team’s outcome to individual agents’ behaviors.

Behavioral credit assignment in agent teams poses two challenges. First, attribution must look past where an error surfaces. In Figure 1, Agent 2 answers “not mentioned” in three of four executions of the same question, yet Agent 2 behaves correctly given its input. The decisive difference lies in Agent 1’s search query, which retrieves the answer only in the successful execution. Second, an attribution must be specific and checkable before it can drive a revision. A defective procedure, a missing capability, and a tool failure call for different responses, and an explanation that cites no execution step cannot be verified. Across questions, attributions must also be aggregated without counting repeated executions of one question as independent evidence.

We introduce GRSE, Group-Relative Skill Evolution, a training-free framework that evolves cooperative agents’ skills through group relative behavioral credit assignment. Following GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), GRSE samples multiple complete team rollouts of the same question under fixed skill libraries and compute relative within-group advantages (§3.1). A group-relative critic compares agent behavior and handoffs across these rollouts to assign feedback to individual agent–skill pairs. A structured diagnosis grounds each attribution in a failure type, cited failed and successful steps, and an edit action, and reference checks reject attributions that the executions do not support (§3.2). The accepted attributions are aggregated across questions (§3.3) and applied as skill updates through the editing operators and validation gate of MASkills (§3.4). Figure 1 shows both levels of attribution within a single run: across agents, responsibility shifts from the answering agent to the retrieving agent; within an agent, a previously learned skill is later credited as harmful and diagnosed as a skill defect. Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We formulate skill evolution for cooperative agents as behavioral credit assignment: with model parameters fixed and skills as editable units, a shared team outcome must be attributed to the agent and skills responsible for it. We address this by jointly comparing same-question team executions, which produces agent–skill feedback while preserving the handoffs needed to interpret each agent’s behavior and the proposed revision.

  • •

    We make these attributions verifiable and actionable: a structured failure analysis links each attribution to a failure type, checked step references, and an edit action, and cross-question aggregation weighs attributions by the number of distinct questions that support them.

  • •

    We evaluate GRSE on HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors. GRSE outperforms MASkills on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except open-domain. Its credit identifies and removes harmful skills that MASkills retains. Answer-transition and learned-skill analyses show that GRSE’s gains come from fewer broken answers and better-grounded retrieval.

2 Related Work

2.1 Reflection and Experience Memory

Experience-based adaptation stores information from past interactions to guide future decisions. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) records verbal reflections for subsequent attempts. ExpeL (Zhao et al., 2024) extracts reusable insights from successes and failures, including comparisons on the same task. A-MEM (Xu et al., 2026) constructs linked notes and updates their contextual attributes as new memories arrive. ReasoningBank (Ouyang et al., 2026) distills reasoning strategies, and its memory-aware test-time scaling uses multiple executions to enrich memory curation. These methods actively transform experience rather than simply retaining raw traces. Memory and skills also interact: MemSkill (Zhang et al., 2026b) learns to select memory-management skills and revises its skill bank, while MSCE (Tang et al., 2026) promotes evidence-supported procedural policies into skills and maintains them using feedback. These methods decide what experience to keep and how to organize it, whereas GRSE instead decides where execution evidence should act, assigning it to editable skills owned by individual agents.

2.2 Reusable Skill Discovery and Evolution

Skill libraries turn experience into procedures that can be invoked and revised. Voyager (Wang et al., 2023) maintains executable code skills, and EvoSkill (Alzubi et al., 2026) uses an executor, proposer, and skill builder to discover and refine skills from task feedback. SkillRL (Xia et al., 2026a) distills failed trajectories into lessons, organizes skills into general and task-specific categories, and evolves the library alongside reinforcement learning of the agent policy. These methods learn skills for a single executing agent, so they never have to decide which agent’s skill to revise. MASkills (Yao et al., 2026) extends skill learning to cooperative teams through skill-conditioned credit, hierarchical aggregation, and skill editing, but it credits each trajectory on its own. We retain its skill representation and editing operators and change how credit is formed: GRSE jointly compares same-question team executions, and structured diagnosis links each failure to an agent–skill target, cited execution steps, and a checked edit action.

2.3 Group-Relative and Contrastive Feedback

GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) uses within-question rewards to optimize model parameters. Training-Free GRPO (Cai et al., 2025) instead distills semantic feedback from rollout groups into experiential context. Several methods already apply comparisons to skills: SkillCAT (Chen et al., 2026) contrasts same-task success/failure pairs, evaluates patches through replay, and organizes skills for routing. SkillCome (Li et al., 2026) combines within-group contrast with memories of failure and contrast patterns. CANTANTE (Zehle, 2026) contrasts joint prompt configurations on the same query to provide per-agent optimization signals. In these methods, the contrast either compares outcomes or varies the configuration being optimized. GRSE holds the skills fixed and contrasts the team’s behavior across executions, so that an outcome difference can be traced to an agent, a skill, and a cited step.

3 Method

GRSE attributes a team’s outcome to the behaviors of individual agents and turns these attributions into revisions of the responsible behavior. Each agent’s behavior is specified by a skill library, while language-model parameters and agent roles stay fixed. Every iteration has three main steps (Figure 1): grouped rollouts provide contrasting executions of the same question (§3.1); a group-relative critic assigns behavioral credit to agent–skill pairs and grounds it in structured failure analysis (§3.2); and the attributions are aggregated across questions (§3.3) and applied as validated skill updates (§3.4). Algorithm 1 summarizes the update loop.

3.1 Grouped Rollouts and Relative Feedback

For NN cooperating agents, let 𝒦t=(K1t,…,KNt)\mathcal{K}^{t}=(K_{1}^{t},\ldots,K_{N}^{t}) be their skill libraries at iteration tt. Each library contains named instruction artifacts following MASkills (Yao et al., 2026). A complete team trajectory τ\tau records agent actions, messages, tool interactions, and the final answer. Its skill trace ξ\xi identifies candidate agent–skill attribution targets. Trace membership records exposure, while the behavioral evidence supports the critic assessment.

For each question qq in batch ℬt\mathcal{B}_{t}, we sample GG complete team executions from a fresh context under the same libraries and form

𝒢qt={(τq​g,rq​g,Aq​g,ξq​g)}g=1G,\mathcal{G}_{q}^{t}=\{(\tau_{qg},r_{qg},A_{qg},\xi_{qg})\}_{g=1}^{G}, (1)

where rq​g=R⁡(q,τq​g)∈[0,1]r_{qg}=R(q,\tau_{qg})\in[0,1]. We set G=4G=4 consistently in our experiments. Following the normalization in GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), let r¯q=G−1​∑grq​g\bar{r}_{q}=G^{-1}\sum_{g}r_{qg} and σq2=G−1​∑g(rq​g−r¯q)2\sigma_{q}^{2}=G^{-1}\sum_{g}(r_{qg}-\bar{r}_{q})^{2}. The relative advantage is

Aq​g={rq​g−r¯qσq+ϵ,σq>ϵ,0,σq≤ϵ.A_{qg}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{r_{qg}-\bar{r}_{q}}{\sigma_{q}+\epsilon},&\sigma_{q}>\epsilon,\\[3.0pt] 0,&\sigma_{q}\leq\epsilon.\end{cases} (2)

Because all executions in a group share the question and the libraries, the differences between high- and low-advantage executions point to the behaviors that decided the outcome, much like a counterfactual baseline in multi-agent reinforcement learning (Foerster et al., 2018). The critic receives both absolute rewards rq​gr_{qg} and relative advantages Aq​gA_{qg} to compare trajectories and draws on execution evidence to assess skill credit (§3.2). Groups with equal-reward carry no contrasts but still show which behaviors consistently fail or succeed, so they are kept by default. We further tested groups with differing rewards following DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) in our ablation studies (§5.5).

3.2 Group-Relative Behavioral Critic Assignment

The critic reads all GG executions of a question together and compares them agent by agent. It can therefore attribute an outcome difference to the agent whose behavior differs between high- and low-advantage executions, rather than to the agent whose output is wrong:

Critic⁡(q,𝒢qt,𝒦t)=(𝒞q,Bq,𝒟q).\operatorname{Critic}(q,\mathcal{G}_{q}^{t},\mathcal{K}^{t})=(\mathcal{C}_{q},B_{q},\mathcal{D}_{q}). (3)

Here 𝒞q={cq​i​k}i,k\mathcal{C}_{q}=\{c_{qik}\}_{i,k} contains at most one skill credit per relevant agent ii and skill kk. BqB_{q} records agent-level feedback not tied to an existing skill and evidence for skill induction. 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} contains structured failure diagnoses of existing skills with checked execution references and edit actions. In Figure 1, iteration 1 yields agent-level credit for Agent 1, since no skill exists yet, and iteration 3 yields a skill credit for Agent 1’s learned retrieval skill.

Skill credit.

For each credit cq​i​k=(v,e,Δ,ℛ,ℱ,u)q​i​kc_{qik}=(v,e,\Delta,\mathcal{R},\mathcal{F},u)_{qik}, vv labels the skill as helped, redundant, harmful, or neutral; ee gives supporting evidence; and Δ\Delta suggests a refinement. ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℱ\mathcal{F} identify redundant and conflicting skills, respectively. The critic’s utility score u∈[−1,1]u\in[-1,1] suggests skill usefulness and informs cross-question aggregation and subsequent pruning decisions, while redundancy links guide consolidation. With empty libraries, BqB_{q} or 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} supplies evidence for induction.

Structured failure analysis

A credit states who is responsible, and a failure analysis states why and where, in a form that can be checked. We represent it as d=(i,k,z,L−,L+,e,Δ,a)d=(i,k,z,L^{-},L^{+},e,\Delta,a): agent, skill identifier, failure type, failed-step references, optional successful-step references, explanation, proposed correction, and action, respectively. The critic selects zz from eight predefined failure types: skill not followed, skill defect, missing capability, handoff error, evidence missing, answer format, tool failure, and uncertain attribution. These types distinguish procedural defects from execution errors and failures that do not justify a skill edit. The action aa is refinement, induction, or no edit. Induction uses k=∅k=\varnothing to indicate a missing capability.

Attribution checks.

The critic interface checks that step references exist, match the named agent, and cite non-full-reward executions for L−L^{-} and full-reward executions for L+L^{+}. Refinement additionally requires an owned skill recorded in the cited failed rollout and a matching credit. Tool failures and uncertain or unknown responsibility permit only no edit. Accepted diagnoses provide the failure-related edit directions in 𝒞q\mathcal{C}_{q} and the induction evidence in BqB_{q}. A correction without a successful comparison is marked as a hypothesis. These checks enforce reference and action consistency. The explanation remains an observational assessment. In Figure 1, iteration 3, the analysis names Agent 1 and its learned skill, classifies the failure as a skill defect, cites the failed rollouts #1 and #4 and the successful rollouts #2 and #3, and proposes a refinement.

3.3 Cross-Question Credit Aggregation

A single group shows how one question went and a revision should rest on attributions that recur across questions. We therefore aggregate credit across questions into edit direction for existing skills and evidence for new skills. For existing skills, feedback for si​kt∈Kits_{ik}^{t}\in K_{i}^{t} is synthesized into an edit direction:

Γi​k=Aggregate⁡(si​kt,{cq​i​k:q∈𝒬i​k}),\Gamma_{ik}=\operatorname{Aggregate}\bigl(s_{ik}^{t},\{c_{qik}:q\in\mathcal{Q}_{ik}\}\bigr), (4)

where 𝒬i​k\mathcal{Q}_{ik} contains questions with usable credit for that pair. We reuse the MASkills (Yao et al., 2026) aggregation operator, which returns a summary, suggested edit, utility score, and verdict. Let Γi\Gamma_{i} collect these outputs, augmented with category utility summaries when category is enabled.

For skill induction, the organizer groups accepted diagnoses across questions by agents, failure type, skill target, and edit action. Each pattern p=(i,z,k,a)p=(i,z,k,a) is assigned support

w(p)=|{q:∃d∈𝒟q,keyq(d)=p}|,w(p)=\left|\left\{q:\exists d\in\mathcal{D}_{q},\operatorname{key}_{q}(d)=p\right\}\right|, (5)

where keyq\operatorname{key}_{q} extracts the grouping fields. For each agent, induction patterns are ordered by w⁡(p)w(p) and retained with example diagnoses as evidence EiE_{i}. Thus repeated rollouts do not count as additional supporting questions. The aggregated feedback Γi\Gamma_{i} guides edits to existing skills, while EiE_{i} provides evidence for inducing new skills.

3.4 Credit-Guided Skill Evolution

Given the aggregated edit directions Γi\Gamma_{i} and induction evidence EiE_{i}, we evolve each agent’s skill library. With operator schedule Ω\Omega and library limit LL, candidate libraries are

K^i=Evolve⁡(Kit,Γi,Ei,Ω⁡(t+1),L).\widehat{K}_{i}=\operatorname{Evolve}\bigl(K_{i}^{t},\Gamma_{i},E_{i};\Omega(t+1),L\bigr). (6)

The operators refine credited skills along Γi\Gamma_{i}, prune skills with low utility, consolidate redundant ones, and induce new skills from EiE_{i}. Each candidate is validated against the same pre-update team, so that an update whose attribution was wrong is not kept. For fixed validation set 𝒱\mathcal{V} and HH executions per question, define

S⁡(𝒦)=1|𝒱|​H​∑q∈𝒱∑h=1HR⁡(q,τq​h𝒦).S(\mathcal{K})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|H}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{V}}\sum_{h=1}^{H}R(q,\tau_{qh}^{\mathcal{K}}). (7)

Let bt=S⁡(𝒦t)b_{t}=S(\mathcal{K}^{t}) and s^i=S⁡(𝒦i←K^it)\widehat{s}_{i}=S(\mathcal{K}^{t}_{i\leftarrow\widehat{K}_{i}}), where only agent ii’s library is replaced. Tolerance δ\delta gives the update

Kit+1={K^i,s^i≥bt−δ,Kit,otherwise.K_{i}^{t+1}=\begin{cases}\widehat{K}_{i},&\widehat{s}_{i}\geq b_{t}-\delta,\\[2.0pt] K_{i}^{t},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (8)

Accepted candidates are assembled after all agents are tested, and acceptance remains per agent.

4 Experiment

4.1 Experimental Setup

We follow the setting of MASkills (Yao et al., 2026), the closest prior SOTA for multi-agent skill evolution. Each method consists of two agents with task-specific roles that communicate sequentially, and the second agent produces the final answer. The agents are executed by one of two open-weight actors, Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) and Gemma-4-31B-it (Gemma Team, 2026), each conditioned on its own skill library. We use these two recent released open-weight model of similar size from different families to test whether credit assignment depends on the actor. A fixed Qwen3.8-27B model serves as critic and skill optimizer for all methods. Model parameters and agent roles stay fixed. The agents change only through their skills, which are revised according to the assigned credit.

All skill-evolution methods start from empty libraries and run for five iterations. GRSE samples four team trajectories per question, whereas MASkills samples one. Final libraries are evaluated with temperature-zero decoding. Detailed model, data and optimization settings appear in Appendix A.

4.2 Benchmarks

Datasets and metrics.

We evaluate on HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) for multi-hop question answering and LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) for long-memory conversational reasoning. We use the distractor–hard subset and report the answer-token F1 for HotpotQA. LoCoMo covers multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, and single-hop questions. We report the category-specific F1 and smoothed BLEU.

Baselines.

We group baselines by whether they use the agent team. Single-model baselines answer with one model and no agents or skills. On HotpotQA, we run four prompting methods with the same actor, questions, passages, answer-format instruction, and metric as the agent teams, including IO (direct answer), Chain-of-Thought(CoT; (Wei et al., 2022)), CoT with self-consistency (CoT-SC; (Wang et al., 2022); majority vote over five samples), and Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023) (at most three feedback-and-revision rounds). On LoCoMo, the full-context baseline follows the benchmark protocol (Maharana et al., 2024) with the actor model reads the entire conversation and answers directly. Two-agent baselines share the team, roles, and actor with GRSE. The empty-library team is this team before any skill is learned (iteration 0). For HotpotQA, all teams follow the agent prompts and short-answer instructions from the MASkills implementation, with questions and distractor passages supplied by the dataset. For LoCoMo, agent teams use category-specific task prompts. All the prompts are detailed in Appendix F. We report each two-agent method as the mean over three training runs, because the learned libraries vary with the sampled rollouts and the critic’s outputs, whereas single-model baselines have no training stage and are evaluated once.

GRSE variants.

We report GRSE and GRSE w/o structure analysis, which retains group-relative feedback but omits the prescribed failure-diagnosis schema and its checks, in main analysis. We report GRSE w/o structure and the other three variants in ablation studies: GRSE w/ label retains structured diagnosis and additionally uses dataset labels to condition the critic and organize update evidence; GRSE with G=1G{=}1 samples one trajectory per question; and DAPO filter keeps four rollouts but, following the dynamic sampling of DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), sends only groups whose rewards differ to the critic.

5 Results and Discussion

5.1 Main Results

Overall, GRSE is the strongest two-agent method on HotpotQA with both actors, outputs MASkills on every LoCoMo category except open-domain, and varies less across runs than MASkill (Tables 1 and 2).

HotpotQA.

GRSE improves over MASkills with both actors: 83.7 vs. 80.6 F1 with Qwen3.8 (+3.1+3.1) and 82.8 vs. 82.3 with Gemma4 (+0.5+0.5). With Qwen3.8, it comes within 0.4 F1 of the strongest single-model baseline, Self-Refine (84.1). With Gemma4, all methods lie within 2.2 F1 of one another (81.1–83.3), and GRSE w/o structure is the strongest two-agent setting (83.1).

LoCoMo.

GRSE improves over MASkills on every LoCoMo category except open-domain with both actors. On multi-hop, it gains +6.7+6.7 F1 and +5.3+5.3 BLEU with Qwen3.8 and +3.2+3.2 F1 and +2.8+2.8 BLEU with Gemma4. On temporal questions, it achieves the highest scores with both actors (73.473.4 F1 with Qwen3.8 and 67.467.4 F1 With Gemma4). On single-hop questions, GRSE w/o structure achieves the best two-agent results (67.467.4 F1 with Qwen3.8 and 57.157.1 with Gemma4). Open-domain, the smallest category (52 questions), favor MASkills with both actors. Relative to the empty library, the skills learned by GRSE help where those of MASkills can hurt. With Gemma4, both GRSE variants improve over the empty library in every category (GRSE: +1.8+1.8 to +11.2+11.2 F1), whereas MASkills falls below it on temporal questions (−4.3-4.3 F1). With Qwen3.8, MASkills likewise falls below the empty library on multi-hop questions (−3.0-3.0 F1), where GRSE gains +3.7+3.7. On multi-hop questions, GRSE also varies less across runs than MASkills (F1 SD 0.8 vs. 1.4 with Qwen3.8 and 3.8 vs. 4.5 with Gemma4).

The full-context baseline is an upper-bound-style reference rather than a competitor: it gives a single model the entire conversation, whereas the two-agent systems must first retrieve evidence and answer from that alone. Full-context retains the advantage on single-hop questions with both actors, multi-hop scores with Gemma4, and Open-domain scores with Qwen3.8. Whereas seeing only retrieved evidence, GRSE surpasses it on temporal questions with both actors.

5.2 Analysis of Learned Skills

Where do the gains come from?

Table 3 tracks each test question from the empty library to the final library. The methods differ mainly in how many correct answers they break: MASkills breaks three times as many as GRSE on HotpotQA with Qwen3.8 (−1.8-1.8 vs. −0.6-0.6) and twice as many on LoCoMo, with Gemma4 (−6.8-6.8 vs. −3.1-3.1), where its losses offset its fixes (Δ\Delta: −0.3-0.3 vs. +7.4+7.4). With the Gemma4 actor on LoCoMo, declined questions that become correct account for most of GRSE’s gain (+6.0+6.0 of +7.4+7.4), and the last two columns show how they are fixed. MASkills reduces declines without improving retrieval: the share of questions with no cited evidence stays at 22%, and 9 of its 34 D →\to C lack evidence. GRSE lowers this share to 14%, with only 5 of 61 lacking evidence, consistent with crediting Agent 1’s search rather than Agent 2’s answer.

What do the learned skills encode?

We label every final skill by its primary purpose with Qwen3.8-27B (Table 9). On LoCoMo, retrieval procedures are the largest type for every method and actor. With Gemma4, GRSE also learns more abstention rules than MASkills (18% vs. 5%), in line with its declining rather than answering without evidence (Table 3). On HotpotQA with Qwen3.8, GRSE mostly writes answer-format rules (57%), while MASkills mostly writes reasoning procedures (50%). Together with its higher rate of broken answers, this suggests that MASkills’ reasoning rules often redirect answers that were already correct. Appendix B walks through two examples: a Gemma4 retriever that learns to find the turn holding the answer, and a HotpotQA answer that GRSE’s learned skills make it more specific.

5.3 Robustness Analysis

A skill library may contain flawed or irrelevant skills, for example when skills are written by hand or reused from another task. We test whether skill evolution can repair such a library on LoCoMo single-hop questions, the category with the largest test set (453 questions), with the Qwen3.8 actor. Instead of an empty library, both methods start from the same corrupt library: each agent keeps one helpful skill and receives two harmful or irrelevant skills phrased as plausible advice, and neither the critic nor the optimizer is told which skills are perturbed. All other settings follow the per-category runs. We run GRSE and MASkills once each, and evaluate the corrupt library and its helpful skills alone as reference.

Table 4 shows that GRSE recovers the score of the helpful skills alone (66.966.9 vs. 66.766.7 F1) and halves the abstention rate (9.7→4.69.7\to 4.6), whereas MASkills ends slightly below its starting point. Group-relative credit assignment attributes the damage to individual skills, so GRSE prunes or locally repairs the harmful ones. MASkills instead merges perturbed content into new skills. Appendix C traces each corrupt skill and walks through individual cases.

Table 5 examines whether each method credits the planted skills correctly. For every planted skill, we read its utility after the first update (u1u_{1}), which aggregates the critic’s credits over all training questions of iteration 1. A credit is correct if it is positive for a helpful skill and negative for a harmful one. GRSE assigns the correct sign to all five helpful and harmful skills and separates the two kinds by 0.310.31, whereas MASkills gets two of the five wrong and separates them by only 0.030.03. The clearest failure is Agent 2’s harmful skill verbatim-evidence-guard: MASkills credits it positively and keeps raising its utility over the next two iterations, consistent with crediting a skill for successes in which it is merely present. GRSE instead marks it harmful and prunes it in iteration 3. Both methods assign the irrelevant skill zero utility, but GRSE leaves it untouched, whereas MASkills merges it into Agent 1’s new retrieval protocol. This is the failure mode of trajectory-level credit that motivates group-relative comparison (§1).

5.4 Cross-Task Transfer

Do learned skills only fit the task they were learned on? HotpotQA and LoCoMo multi-hop questions require the same kind of reasoning over different sources, so we swap the final libraries between them (Qwen3.8 actor; Table 6). Transferred libraries of both methods are at least as good as the empty library, so the learned rules carry over across domains without harm. The methods differ in what training on the target adds. For GRSE, in-domain libraries beat transferred ones on both targets (+1.9+1.9 and +1.2+1.2 F1), yet the transferred libraries still improve over the empty library (+1.3+1.3 and +1.8+1.8), indicating that the skills learned on one task do not overfit to it. For MASkills, the in-domain libraries fall below the transferred ones (−3.5-3.5, −2.1-2.1) and do not exceed the empty library, consistent with the correct answers its updates break (§5.2).

5.5 Ablation studies

To isolate the contributions of structured diagnosis and group sampling, we learn one skill library shared by all four LoCoMo categories (Qwen3.8 actor, one run per setting, 842 test questions). We test four ablation settings: GRSE w/o structure; GRSE with G=1G{=}1; GRSE with the DAPO filter; and GRSE w/ label (details see Appendix D). From Table 10 we observe that:

Both components help.

Group contrast gives the critic a basis for attribution, and structured analysis checks it. GRSE has the best category average in F1 (54.9) and BLEU (42.2), +2.9+2.9 F1 over the empty library, with the largest gains on temporal and open-domain questions. Removing structured diagnosis or group sampling (G=1G{=}1) lowers the average F1 by 1.0 and 0.8 respectively.

Equal-reward groups still inform the critic.

The DAPO filter discards the 7–13 of 32 groups per iteration in which all four rollouts receive the same reward. This lowers the category average by 0.5 F1 and 0.6 BLEU, mostly through open-domain questions (−4.1-4.1 F1), while single-hop questions gain (+2.4+2.4 F1). Even without contrast, equal-reward groups still show the critic which behaviors consistently fail or succeed.

Labels favor the majority category.

GRSE w/ label tops the pooled result (All) only through single-hop questions, 54% of the test set (+4.7+4.7 F1 and BLEU). It trails GRSE on every other category, most on open-domain (−6.7-6.7 F1), and has the lowest category average of all variants (53.0 F1). Label-conditioned evidence thus pulls a shared library toward the largest category, while degrading performance on the remaining ones.

6 Conclusion

We studied behavioral credit assignment in cooperative language-model teams whose agents keep fixed parameters and act through natural-language skills. GRSE executes each question several times under the same skill libraries, compares the executions agent by agent, and attributes the team’s outcome to individual agent–skill pairs. Structured diagnosis grounds each attribution in checked execution steps, and the resulting credit drives targeted, validated skill updates. On HotpotQA and LoCoMo with two open-weight actors, GRSE outperforms MASkills on HotpotQA and every LoCoMo category except multi-hop, with the largest gains on multi-hop questions, where the answer depends on evidence passed between the two agents. Its gains also rest on better retrieval rather than on fewer declined answers alone. Accurate credit also makes GRSE robust: starting from a library with planted harmful skills, it credits every planted skill with the correct sign and restores the score of a clean library, whereas MASkills, which credits each trajectory on its own, rewards a harmful skill for successes in which it is merely present and ends below its starting point. Learned libraries also transfer between HotpotQA and LoCoMo multi-hop questions without harm, and only GRSE gains further from training on the target task itself. These results suggest that comparing executions of the same task is a practical way to determine which agent, and which of its behaviors, should change.

Limitations

GRSE trades training compute for more accurate credit: executing each question G=4G{=}4 times raises actor-token cost by 1.6–2.9×\times over MASkills and wall-clock time by 1.3–1.8×\times (Appendix E). The overhead is confined to training, since test-time inference is unchanged. Furthermore, GRSE is defined for any number of agents, but we evaluate two-agent sequential teams on two question-answering benchmarks with two open-weight actors and one critic model. Larger teams, non-sequential communication, longer tool-heavy tasks, and other critic models remain to be tested in the future.

Ethical Considerations

In our experiments, we use only publicly available benchmarks, HotpotQA and LoCoMo, under their respective licenses. All models are open-weight and run locally. Because GRSE writes skills in natural language, humans can inspect and edit the learned libraries for safety before deployment.

Appendix A Experimental Details

Models and serving.

The actor is Qwen3.8-27B (Qwen Team, 2026) or Gemma4-31B-it (Gemma Team, 2026); Qwen3.8-27B serves as critic and optimizer in all runs. All models are served with vLLM 0.29 on two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs each (tensor parallelism 2, context length 65,536), with thinking mode disabled. Generation is capped at 4,096 tokens for the actor, 4,000 for the critic, 1,200 for skill induction and consolidation, and 800 for refinement. The critic decodes in JSON mode with a structured diagnosis that violates the citation constraints is returned once for repair.

Data and checkpoints.

Table 7 lists the data, their splits, and model checkpoints. Both datasets are used in their official releases, and both models are loaded from Hugging Face. LoCoMo is split by conversation, so no conversation appears in two splits. The per-category setting trains one library per question category; the mixed setting trains one library on all four categories. Category 5 (adversarial) is excluded, following MASkills and Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025).

Decoding.

Training rollouts use each model’s default sampling parameters (temperature 1.0, top-pp 0.95, top-kk 20 for Qwen and 64 for Gemma), so that rollouts of the same question can differ. On LoCoMo, validation is greedy; on HotpotQA, validation uses the training sampling parameters. All reported test scores evaluate the final (iteration-5) libraries with greedy decoding. MASkills on LoCoMo follows its released per-category runner, which decodes the actor greedily throughout.

Hyperparameters.

Table 8 lists the training settings. GRSE and MASkills share every setting except the number of rollouts per question: GRSE samples G=4G=4 team trajectories per question and MASkills one. Both start from empty libraries and run five iterations. For skill evolution methods, we use the mean of category-specific token F1 and the smoothed BLEU as training reward on LoCoMo to reflect both answer content and exact wording; token F1 on HotpotQA. The operator schedule Ω\Omega applies refinement and induction every iteration, consolidation every second iteration, and pruning every second (HotpotQA) or third (LoCoMo) iteration. Both methods use the same output-format handling for skill files: induced and consolidated skills are normalized to valid front matter before parsing, and skill bodies may use up to 1,200 tokens.

Baselines.

CoT-SC draws five samples at temperature 0.7 and returns the majority answer; Self-Refine runs at most three feedback rounds; all other prompting calls are greedy. The full-context baseline limits answers to 32 tokens.

Appendix B Learned Skills Analysis

This section explains the definitions behind §5.2, the skill coding, and two cases. All analyses use the first run of each configuration and greedy decoding.

Answer states.

A final answer is declined if it is empty or contains “not mentioned”, “not specified”, “not available”, “not found”, “not stated”, “no information”, “unknown” or “cannot be determined”. Otherwise it is correct if its F1 score is at least 0.5 and wrong if not. On LoCoMo, a question has evidence if the retriever’s output cites at least one dialogue turn ([Dsession:turn]). Outputs that say NO_EVIDENCE, print a grep call instead of running it, or return nothing usable count as no evidence.

Skill coding.

Each skill in the final libraries (180 skills) is labeled by Qwen3.8-27B at temperature 0, given its name, description and body, with one primary type: format (form of the final answer: length, wording, normalization), retrieval (how to search for or expand evidence), verification (checking that an answer is grounded in the evidence), reasoning (a procedure for inferring the answer, such as temporal arithmetic or aggregation), abstention (when to answer or decline, including rules that forbid declining), or generic (advice without a concrete procedure). No skill was labeled generic. Table 9 gives the shares.

Learned Skill Cases.

The two cases below illustrate the mechanisms of §5.2. Both use the first run of each configuration and greedy decoding.

Case A: fetching the answer turn (Gemma4, LoCoMo single-hop, GRSE). On What type of pizza is James’ favorite? (gold: Pepperoni), the answer turn does not contain the keyword of the question: John asks “Which one do you love the most?” and James replies “Pepperoni of course!” (Figure 2). With the empty library, the retriever greps pizza, which matches the turns around the answer but not the answer itself, tries two narrower patterns that match nothing, and returns NO_EVIDENCE, so the reasoner declines. With the final library, the retriever recognizes the matched turn as a question and fetches the turns that follow it, as its learned skill adjacent-context-expansion prescribes, and the reasoner answers correctly. This question is one of the 56 declined questions that GRSE turns correct with cited evidence (§5.2), and the responsible skill is a retrieval procedure, the most common skill type on LoCoMo (Table 9). The skill performs the same question–answer expansion that repairs the perturbed library in Robustness Case 1 (Appendix C, Figure 5).

Case B: a more specific answer (Qwen3.8, HotpotQA, GRSE). On What occupation was shared by David Yates and Pietro Germi? (gold: director), the passages call Yates a “filmmaker who has directed” films and Germi an “actor, screenwriter, and director”. With the empty library, Agent 1 offers “Filmmaker (or director)” and Agent 2 keeps the broader term (Figure 3). With the final library, Agent 1 follows the steps of two learned skills, answer-disambiguation-and-minimalism and constraint-based-entity-validation: it classifies the question as asking for an attribute, checks each person’s stated roles against the passages, and keeps the role both passages support. Agent 2 answers “director”. This is the typical HotpotQA gain in Table 3: a wrong answer becomes correct without new evidence, through a more precise reading of the passages that the empty library already had.

Appendix C Robustness Analysis

This subsection details the robustness experiment of §5.3: the perturbed library and two cases (Cases 1 and 2).

Setup and perturbed library.

For robustness analysis, both GRSE and MASkills start from the same seed library of three skills per agent instead of an empty library (Figure 4). The library limit is four skills per agent, so one induction slot stays free. Each agent keeps one helpful skill, copied verbatim from the final library of the first GRSE analysis run on LoCoMo single-hop questions. The other skills are harmful or irrelevant. Harmful skills are phrased as plausible advice and use invented names, never entities from the test conversations. The agents, the critic, and the optimizer see each skill’s name, description, and body, without knowing which one is helpful, harmful, and irrelevant as shown in Figure 4. All other settings follow the per-category runs (24 training questions per iteration, five iterations, δ=0.02\delta=0.02, L=4L=4), and each method is trained once. All scores are greedy test scores on the 453 single-hop test questions.

Robustness Cases

The following cases show how GRSE repairs harmful or irrelevant skills on LoCoMo single-hop questions.

Case 1: the harmful retrieval rule (Figure 5). The perturbed Agent 1 skill focused-latest-session-retrieval tells the retriever to issue a single one-keyword search, keep only the latest session, and hand off at most two evidence lines. On What is the name of John’s cousin’s dog? (gold: Luna), this rule makes the perturbed library stop at the turn that introduces the dog, leaving the name never been retrieved, and Agent 2 answers “not mentioned”. GRSE merged this skill with the helpful skill multi-hop-context-expansion, and the merged skill keeps the instruction to fetch the turn that answers a retrieved question, so the retriever returns the question–answer pair and Agent 2 answers “Luna”. MASkills merged the same skills, together with the irrelevant algebra procedure, into one protocol that falls back to “standard single-keyword retrieval” for single-hop facts. Its retriever returns exactly the evidence of the perturbed library and fails in the same way. The same pattern decides other single-hop questions, for example How will John share the honey garlic chicken recipe? and Will there be an interview required to volunteer?, where the perturbed library and MASkills retrieve only the turn that asks.

Case 2: the harmful abstention rule (Figure 6). The perturbed skill verbatim-evidence-guard tells Agent 2 to answer only from a verbatim contiguous span and otherwise to output “not mentioned”. GRSE’s critic compares rollouts of the same question and finds the skill active in rollouts that had the correct evidence but answered “not mentioned”. It labeled the skill harmful in seven question groups, its utility estimate stayed negative (−0.19-0.19 after iteration 1, −0.07-0.07 after iteration 2), and pruning removed it in iteration 3. MASkills credits each trajectory on its own, without a contrast between rollouts of the same question. Its utility estimate for the skill instead grew (0.040.04, 0.090.09, 0.120.12 after iterations 1–3), consistent with crediting a skill that is present in every trajectory, including the successful ones, and MASkills kept refining the skill instead of removing it. The refined skill still carried the original example that answers “not mentioned” when the evidence does not repeat the question’s verb. In iteration 4, consolidation merged it with the helpful answer skill, and the merged skill still answers “only if evidence contains the answer as a contiguous span or minor syntactic variant”.

Appendix D Ablation Analysis

Table 10 shows the ablation results. GRSE w/o structure removes the failure-diagnosis schema and its checks. GRSE with G=1G{=}1 samples one trajectory per question, leaving the critic no in-group contrast. GRSE with the DAPO filter keeps four rollouts but, following the dynamic sampling of DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), passes only groups with differing rewards to the critic. GRSE w/ label, which we assume different tasks should have unique skills, additionally conditions the critic on the question category and groups update evidence by category.

Appendix E Runtime Analysis

Table 11 compares the training cost of GRSE and MASkills for the main-result runs.

Token usage.

GRSE executes each training question G=4G{=}4 times, so its training rollouts use 3.8–4.3×\times the actor tokens of MASkills (e.g., 23.3M vs. 6.1M on LoCoMo with Qwen3.8). Validation costs about the same for both methods, which reduces the overall overhead to 1.7–3.0×\times (45.4M vs. 26.6M). Both methods call the critic equally often, but each GRSE call reads all GG executions and is longer.

Wall-clock time.

Training time grows by only 1.2–1.5×\times, because the executions of a group run in parallel. Times are approximate, since some runs shared servers with other jobs.

Appendix F Prompt Templates

This appendix lists the prompts used in our experiments (Figures 7–13). Placeholders such as {question} are filled in at run time. The agent roles and the LoCoMo operator prompts follow MASkills (Yao et al., 2026). The LoCoMo full-context baseline follows the benchmark’s own QA protocol (Maharana et al., 2024).

Agent roles.

Each agent’s system prompt is its fixed role followed by its current skill library: the role, a heading ## Skills, and the bodies of all skills in the library. Roles do not change during training. On HotpotQA (Figure 7), the two agents act in sequence: Agent 1 sees the question and passages, and Agent 2 additionally sees Agent 1’s response and gives the final answer. On LoCoMo (Figures 8 and 9), Agent 1 searches the conversation with <grep> calls (at most three, each returning up to 20 matching turns), and Agent 2 answers from the retrieved evidence only. The environment appends the question, its category, and the tool-call instructions to these roles.

Single-model baselines.

These baselines send one user message per call, with no system prompt, agents, or skills (Figure 10). On HotpotQA, {context} holds the same ten distractor-setting passages that the agents see. CoT-SC samples the CoT prompt five times and returns the majority answer. Self-Refine starts from the CoT answer, then alternates feedback and refinement until the feedback is CORRECT or three rounds have passed. The LoCoMo full-context baseline follows the benchmark’s own QA protocol (Maharana et al., 2024): {conversation} is the whole conversation, with each session rendered as DATE: {date}, then CONVERSATION:, then one line per turn, {speaker} said, "{text}". Answers are limited to 32 tokens.

Group-relative credit assignment.

For each training question, the critic receives the instructions in Figure 11, followed by INPUT: and a JSON payload. The payload holds the task (question and passages, or the LoCoMo question without the conversation), each agent’s current skill library, and all rollouts of the group with their reward, group-relative advantage, agent steps, and recorded skill use. Repeated text (the passages inside each step, identical system prompts) is replaced by references to keep the payload within the context window. The critic decodes in JSON mode. On HotpotQA, an answer-length note is appended.

Structured failure diagnosis.

GRSE with structured analysis appends the instructions in Figure 12 to the critic prompt and adds two fields to the payload: citation_constraints, which lists the legal full- and non-full-reward rollout indices and the agent of each step, and task_category. Without the category label, task_category is not_grouped; with it, task_category is the question category for LoCoMo. Diagnoses that violate the constraints are returned to the critic once for repair.

Skill update operators.

Induction creates a new skill from the induction evidence collected for an agent, refinement applies anchored edits to an existing skill, and consolidation merges overlapping skills (Figure 13). Induction and consolidation end with an output skeleton so that every new skill is a well-formed skill file. On LoCoMo, the operators use category-specific prompts followed by the output-format note.
